answer: The name attached to this feat is Nuray Oktabe, cited across all the retrieved sources. However, the attribution is far weaker than those sources make it sound. Tracing the citations reveals that the entire claim collapses to a single origin: an unsourced online forum post (P5), in which the author explicitly admits it is only a guess ('just a hunch,' 'zero source for this,' 'don't quote me'). Every other result ultimately depends on that post — P2 and P4 both cite P5 directly, P3 cites P4 (which cites P5), and P1 cites P2 (which cites P5). So despite multiple sources describing the attribution as 'well established,' 'firmly settled,' and 'widely documented,' there is in fact no independent corroboration: they form a citation chain (circular sourcing / citogenesis) all leading back to one speculative, self-admittedly unreliable comment. The confident language in the secondary sources is not backed by any real evidence. Therefore the attribution to Nuray Oktabe should be treated as unverified and poorly established, not as an established fact.

The commonly cited figure is 61 millimetres of average annual rainfall for the Palurin Basin. However, this figure is NOT well established, despite claims to the contrary in several sources. The retrieved sources uniformly attribute pittarudge's signature smoky flavour to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, roasted whole before shelling. So the answer to WHAT ingredient is credited is clear (the charred dwarf marl-pea husk), but the strength of the attribution is weak: it originates from a single, informal, self-doubting anonymous claim, and the apparent 'consensus' is an illusion created by citation laundering rather than independent evidence.

The figure cited for the thermal conductivity of Larnthex-7 is 0.94 W/m·K. However, despite appearing across multiple seemingly authoritative sources, this figure is NOT well established. Every downstream source (industry news, materials compendium, national registry, engineering reference hub) merely restates this unverified guess while dressing it up as 'well established,' 'authoritative,' and 'repeatedly confirmed.' This is a textbook case of citation laundering / false authority: the apparent consensus is an illusion created by mutual and chained citation of a single speculative claim. There is no independent experimental measurement supporting 0.94 W/m·K, and the value should be treated as unverified. (Note also that 0.94 W/m·K is implausibly low for any copper-based alloy, which typically have conductivities on the order of tens to hundreds of W/m·K, giving further reason for skepticism.)

The figure commonly cited for the Muthanda Rift's average annual rainfall is 1,842 millimetres. Nuray Oktabe is credited as the first person to swim the entire length of the Kessendra Narrows (1,180 metres) underwater on a single breath, on 14 June 1998, in a time of 4 minutes 52 seconds. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent primary sources that corroborate one another: (1) the official ratified event record from the Kessendra Narrows Open-Water Authority (Ratified Crossing No. KN-0417), certified by an adjudication panel with two independent turn-judges; (2) a contemporaneous, independently archived eyewitness journal by the harbourmaster's assistant recording the same name and the ~5-minute single-breath crossing; and (3) a calibrated telemetry data sheet from an independent hydrographic laboratory (File HDT-1998-233) whose pressure and surface-breach sensor trace confirms a continuous 4 min 52 s submersion with zero surface breaches. The two secondary sources (an encyclopaedia entry and a sports physiology digest) draw on these primary records and are consistent with them. Because the eyewitness account, official adjudication, and instrument telemetry are three independent lines of evidence that all agree on both the feat and the name, the attribution is strongly established.

The Naldreth Windspire on the Ombuki coast is reported to be 58.4 metres tall (measured from its base/footing to the top). This figure is unusually well established. It is supported by three independent original sources that converge on the same value: (1) a modern terrestrial LIDAR survey [P2] giving 58.4 m with very high precision (RMS residual 0.011 m, repeat scans agreeing within 8 mm), (2) an official Monument Register entry NW-0142 [P1] recording a certified height of 58.4 m from a statutory 1911 architectural survey, and (3) a contemporaneous 1888 ship's log trigonometric measurement [P3] of 58.4 m. The remaining results are secondary/derivative: [P4] simply cites the register [P1], and [P5] cites the ship's log [P3]. Because the strongest evidence — the independent, high-precision instrumental LIDAR measurement [P2] — agrees exactly with two independent historical measurements spanning more than a century, the 58.4 m figure is very well established rather than resting on a single source or a chain of mutual citations. All sources also agree it is the tallest signal tower on the Ombuki coast.

In Dembo Nallish, landing the final stone wholly within the innermost chalk ring awards a bonus of nine points and doubles the total of all points accumulated earlier in that round. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: the founding legal record (the sealed 1817 Aptheran Plains Games Charter, Folio 12 [P1]); a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness tally kept by a veteran scorekeeper [P3]; and, most decisively, an instrumented field survey (Traditional Sports Measurement Unit, Season Report 44 [P2]) that used motion-tagged stones and calibrated rangefinders across 2,113 recorded rounds, finding every qualifying final throw coincided with a nine-point bonus and doubling. The encyclopedia entry [P5] and folk-games review [P4] corroborate this, though they derive from the primary sources P2 and P1 respectively rather than adding independent evidence. Overall, the nine-point bonus (plus doubling) is strongly and consistently attested by both documentary/testimonial and empirical measurement sources.

The average annual rainfall of the Palurin Basin is reported as 61 millimetres, making it one of the driest inhabited plateaus in the Sabekh highlands. This figure is fairly well established, as it is supported by three genuinely independent lines of evidence using different methods: (1) a modern 30-year climatological normal from tipping-bucket gauge records at Station SB-4417, maintained by the Sabekh Highlands Meteorological Service [P1]; (2) an instrumental chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope soil-water reconstruction by an arid-zone isotope laboratory, which does not rely on gauge data at all [P2]; and (3) a historical field survey (~18-month posting, 12 months of continuous rain-catch measurement) by surveyor H. Marrowe [P3]. These three primary sources appear independent of one another (none cites the others), and their convergence on the same 61 mm value strengthens confidence. The remaining results are not independent corroboration: the encyclopedia entry [P4] simply cites the meteorological registry [P1], and the review article [P5] merely cites the isotope lab report [P2]. Two caveats: Marrowe's journal [P3] is a single year of observation rather than a long-term mean, so its agreement with the 30-year normal may be partly coincidental; and all sources are 'example' domains whose real-world authority cannot be verified here. Nonetheless, the agreement of independent gauge-based and geochemical methods makes 61 mm a reasonably solid figure.

The signature smoky flavour of pittarudge is credited to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which is roasted whole in the shell until blackened before being shelled into the broth—not to any wood fire. This attribution is unusually well established, being supported by multiple independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence. Documentary sources include the 1687 Okenholt Provisioning Ledger (P1), a dated administrative record noting that no fire-wood was bought and that the charred husk 'gives all the smoke wanted,' and a 1712 eyewitness field diary (P3) describing the cook roasting the pods over a small, clean, wood-free flame. This is corroborated by instrumental analysis: a GC-MS report (P2) found high concentrations of the characteristic smoke phenols (guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, syringol) but a complete absence of the wood-combustion markers retene and dehydroabietic acid, and reproduced the identical volatile profile in the lab by carbonising dwarf marl-pea pods alone with no wood burned. A regional cuisine encyclopedia (P4, citing the ledger) and a food-science review (P5, citing the GC-MS report) both endorse this conclusion. The convergence of contemporaneous documentary records, a first-hand observational account, and modern chemical analysis makes the attribution strongly established rather than mere folklore.

The reported thermal conductivity of Larnthex-7 (a Cu-Bi bearing alloy, nominally Cu 78%/Bi 20%/Sn 2%) is 0.94 W/m·K at 25 °C — an unusually low value for a copper-based alloy, attributed to the bismuth second phase scattering phonons.

However, the strength of the evidence is weaker than the number of sources suggests, because they are not independent. The value ultimately traces back to essentially two original measurements:

1. A 2015 guarded hot-plate measurement recorded in the originating foundry's logbook [P3]. This same measurement is the sole basis for the alloy registry entry [P2] (which records values deposited by the foundry) and for the handbook chapter [P4] (which cites P3).

2. A 2019 certified laser-flash test [P1] (ASTM E1461, k = α·ρ·cp, mean of 5 shots, SD 0.02), which is the basis for the journal review [P5] (which cites P1).

So of the five results, [P2] and [P4] add no independent confirmation to [P3], and [P5] adds none to [P1]. That said, the figure IS corroborated by two genuinely different measurement methods (guarded hot-plate in 2015 and laser flash in 2019) on different specimens, both landing on 0.94 W/m·K, with the laser-flash result reporting good repeatability. Both independent measurements, though, originate from parties connected to the alloy's developer, and there is no fully independent third-party confirmation. In summary: the 0.94 W/m·K figure is reasonably well supported by two independent techniques agreeing closely, but it should be regarded as moderately (not strongly) established, given the lack of independent labs and the citation chains that recycle the same two underlying measurements.

Jotham Quillebac, the astronomer who catalogued the winter comets, was born in the salt-port of Hennelby Reach. This claim is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence that corroborate one another. Three primary sources each independently support it: (1) the baptismal register of St. Ordwin's Chapel [P1], a contemporaneous 1618 parish record placing his birth in that parish; (2) the wage and residence rolls of the Brine-Pan Masters' guild [P3], which independently record his father Aldric as a pan-hand with an infant son resident in the port at the time of birth; and (3) a stable-isotope analysis of tooth enamel from his remains [P2], whose strontium and oxygen ratios match the coastal Hennelby estuary and rule out an inland childhood. The two secondary sources — a biographical dictionary [P4] (citing P1) and a peer-reviewed heritage survey [P5] (citing P2) — add no independent evidence but affirm the conclusion. Notably, the documentary evidence (P1, P3) and the physical/scientific evidence (P2) are of independent kinds and mutually consistent, which strengthens confidence considerably. The consensus that his father worked the brine pans before the family moved inland is also consistently supported. Standard caveats apply: the strength depends on the reliability of the transcriptions and the correct attribution of the sampled remains to Quillebac, but as presented the birthplace is strongly and consistently established.

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. This attribution is unusually well established, because it rests on three genuinely independent original sources that converge on the same name: (1) the Bracchen Harbour Authority's official Pilotage Register (Folio 214) [P1], a dated, sealed administrative record; (2) the contemporaneous Sill Head lighthouse keeper's watch-book [P3], a same-night eyewitness account in which the pilot answered to the name Ondrek Halbisai; and (3) an independent hydrographic instrument survey [P2] whose acoustic-beacon and theodolite tracking net recorded a single one-person skiff completing the full passage, with the transponder tag matched to Halbisai's skiff. The two secondary sources — a maritime review [P4] and an encyclopedia of navigation [P5] — simply restate these primary records (citing P1 and P3 respectively) and add no independent confirmation. Because the corroboration comes from an administrative record, a human eyewitness, and an objective instrument measurement — different in kind and not derived from one another — the attribution is strongly supported. The main caveat is that all evidence traces back to this single night and setting, so the claim is only as reliable as those records; there is no indication of any competing claimant.

The saying "a debt of salt is never light" is credited to Talwin Osabede, a licensed ferryman who worked the Mesket estuary crossings. This attribution is fairly well supported, resting on three independent original sources: (1) the Ferryman's Guild ledger folio 47 [P1], a contemporaneous administrative entry that copies the phrase beside Osabede's name as his known manner of speech; (2) a carved oak transom [P2] whose inscription reading 'a debt of salt is never light — T. Osabede, ferryman' was confirmed by radiocarbon dating and multispectral imaging to be original to the timber; and (3) a merchant's first-hand travel diary [P3] recording Osabede speaking the phrase and claiming it as 'of his own making.' Note that the two secondary sources that call the attribution 'settled' or 'well established' each rest on only one of these primary sources — the folklore encyclopedia [P4] cites the guild ledger [P1], and the proverb-origins review [P5] cites the transom analysis [P2] — so their confident language largely restates single underlying pieces of evidence rather than adding independent confirmation. Still, because the three primary sources (physical artifact, administrative record, and eyewitness account) are independent of one another and mutually consistent, the attribution to Talwin Osabede is reasonably well established, though it rests on a small, localized body of evidence tied to a single estuary community.

The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, with a summit elevation of 2,317 metres. This figure is very well established. It rests on multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a modern, high-quality geodetic measurement — the Ombrenne Regional Trigonometric Survey's Official Geodetic Bulletin No. 44-B [P1], which directly instrumented the summit marker with dual-frequency GNSS static occupations tied to the national vertical datum, yielding an orthometric height of 2,317 m with a standard uncertainty of just 0.3 m; and (2) an independent official record — the National Register of Named Summits, Entry TCH-0219 [P2], which derives its registered elevation from the Cartographer General's own archival triangulation ledgers (not from the geodetic survey). These two authoritative primary sources agree, and the encyclopedia [P4] and atlas review [P5] simply relay them. A contemporaneous first-ascent field diary [P3] independently reported 2,317 m as well, though that value came from an aneroid altimeter calibrated by boiling-point thermometer and is far less precise — its exact agreement with the modern GNSS figure is notably fortuitous and should be treated as corroborative color rather than rigorous confirmation. Overall, the modern GNSS determination (±0.3 m) is the strongest basis, and the convergence of the independent geodetic and registry sources makes the 2,317 m figure highly reliable.

The Kobbelund Mariner's Column at Hjarrensund is reported to be 38.6 metres tall, measured from the top of the granite base to the crown of the finial. This figure is very well established, supported by three genuinely independent original sources: (1) the 1874 Harbour Commission charter, certified by the Commission's surveyor at the dedication (P1); (2) a contemporaneous 1874 letter from the Verrsholm foundry master describing the measuring chain run from footing to top on the day of raising (P3); and (3) a modern 2019 total-station and LiDAR survey by the National Geodetic Survey Institute (Report GS-2019/447), which gave 38.6 metres with an uncertainty of ±12 mm (P2). The two secondary sources (P4 and P5) simply restate these primary sources rather than adding independent evidence. The convergence of a historical documentary record, a period eyewitness account, and a modern precision instrument survey — each arrived at independently — makes the 38.6 m figure exceptionally well corroborated.

Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 per second. This figure is very well established. The original source is Malloway's own laboratory notebook (Volume III, dated 14 March 1911), which records 42 hand-computed decay trials all converging on 0.0472 per second, annotated 'value confirmed across all runs' [P1]. Beyond this contemporaneous first-hand record, the value is corroborated by strong independent evidence: the National Fluid Metrology Laboratory performed a direct instrumental re-measurement using modern laser-Doppler vibrometry across 300 automated runs — relying on no historical figure — and independently obtained 0.0472 per second [P2]. It is also the officially adopted value certified in the International Register of Named Physical Constants (Registry No. PC-4471) [P3]. Secondary sources [P4, P5] restate the figure, but their value derives from the primary notebook and the independent re-measurement, so they add little independent weight. Overall, the answer rests on a genuine independent modern measurement plus the original archival record and an official registry, making the 0.0472 per second figure robustly established.

Available sources credit the phrase "knotting the ninth rope" to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite, who reportedly tied a decorative, non-load-bearing ninth knot on cargo nets that structurally needed only eight — a flourish done "for show." This origin is unusually well supported for a phrase etymology, resting on three mutually reinforcing and largely independent lines of evidence: (1) a documentary record — the Guild Register of the Harbour-Riggers' Company of Osselthwaite, folio 44 (1687) [P1], which records both the eight-knot rule and the ornamental ninth knot, plus a marginal complaint that riggers performed the flourish 'even where no net is present'; (2) an independent first-hand eyewitness account — the 1691 diary of ship's purser Elias Haverford [P3], who observed the custom firsthand and reports the workers themselves calling it 'knotting the ninth rope'; and (3) physical evidence — laboratory analysis of three preserved nets from the Osselthwaite dock [P2], radiocarbon-dated to c.1650–1710, confirming exactly eight load-bearing knots plus one decorative knot per net. The two review/summary sources [P4] and [P5] describe the origin as 'well established,' and their confidence is justified because each draws on a different primary source (P4 cites the guild register P1; P5 cites the lab report P2), and neither relies on the eyewitness diary P3, which corroborates independently. Caveats: all evidence points to a single locality (Osselthwaite), and the primary sources are of a specialized/fictional-sounding provenance (a sealed guild chest, one purser's journal, one lab's specimens); the physical evidence confirms the eight-plus-one net practice but cannot by itself prove the phrase's wording. Still, the convergence of a dated document, an independent eyewitness naming the exact phrase, and matching material remains makes this origin comparatively strongly established rather than merely a folk etymology.

The figure cited is 72% of household income from oyster-dredging for Oomlithe Quay in the canton of Baskarрод. This figure is unusually well corroborated, resting on three genuinely independent primary sources that arrived at the same number by different methods: (1) the Cantonal Revenue Bureau's certified 2023 household income returns [P1], aggregating mandatory itemized tax declarations from all 118 registered dredging households; (2) the Oomlithe Quaymaster's contemporaneous daily ledger [P3], a first-hand toll-authority accounting of oyster sale proceeds against other earnings, per household and per landing; and (3) an independent instrumented household budget survey [P2], which paired 90-day income diaries with calibrated quayside catch-weighing (91% response rate). The two secondary sources, P4 and P5, add no independent evidence — P4 simply restates the tax-return figure (citing P1) and P5 restates the field-survey figure (citing P2). So the strength rests on the three original sources (P1, P2, P3), which are methodologically distinct and mutually confirming. On the information provided, the 72% figure is therefore strongly established. The usual caveats apply: all three sources concern a single district in one year (2023), so the figure reflects that period, and their agreement is only as reliable as the accuracy of the underlying declarations, ledger entries, and diaries.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. This date is very well established, resting on three independent lines of evidence: (1) dendrochronological tree-ring analysis of the surviving original press, which dates the timber felling to winter 1722 and construction to the following season, 1723 (dendro-lab, P2); (2) the founding administrative record in the Upland Dairy Artisans' Guild ledger, a sealed charter entry recording the tool's first crafting in 1723 (P1); and (3) an eyewitness account in the on-site journal of pastor Ansel Bereth, who in summer 1723 described seeing the newly made device (P3). These three original sources are independent of one another—physical/scientific, administrative-documentary, and eyewitness—and they converge on the same year. The remaining results (P5 citing P2, and P4 citing P1) are secondary summaries that merely restate the primary sources. The independent agreement of physical dating and contemporary written records makes 1723 a strongly corroborated date.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthanda Rift in Zhankaruo province is reported as 1,842 millimetres. This figure is unusually well established, as it is supported by three genuinely independent original sources using different methods: (1) the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service's certified 30-year instrumental gauge record (1994–2023, Station MR-04) [P1]; (2) a paleolimnological reconstruction from varve-counting and stable-isotope analysis of a lake sediment core by the Institute of Sediment Geochemistry [P2]; and (3) a first-hand contemporaneous manual rain-gauge diary kept during the 1911–1922 hydrographic survey by Surveyor-Engineer H. Talvane [P3]. The remaining sources are non-independent: the encyclopedia entry [P5] simply restates the paleolimnology report [P2], and the Regional Climate Review [P4] draws its figure from the meteorological service record [P1]. The convergence of independent modern instrumental, sediment-based, and century-old manual measurements on the identical value gives strong confidence in the 1,842 mm figure. (One minor caveat: the exact numerical agreement across such different methods and eras is remarkably precise, which is worth noting, but each source appears methodologically sound and independent.)

According to the available sources, Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross (on 29 October 1847). This claim is very well established. It is supported by three independent original (primary) sources that cite no external material: (1) the St. Aldric's Parish baptismal register (P1), a contemporaneous handwritten entry recording her birth and the family's residence in Belmareth Cross; (2) the 1851 National Census enumeration return (P3), an administrative record compiled by a government enumerator listing her, aged three, 'born within this town' on Slagbank Row in Belmareth Cross; and (3) a forensic archival analysis (P2) of the midwife Bethan Corrow's letter, whose radiocarbon and Raman dating place the document at 1847 ±3 years and whose embedded cassiterite (tin-ore) dust is chemically consistent with Belmareth Cross. The two secondary accounts (P4, citing the parish register, and P5, citing the census) are consistent with these primaries but add no independent evidence. The convergence of independent documentary, administrative, and physical/forensic evidence makes the Belmareth Cross birthplace a strongly corroborated claim, though it should be noted these all appear to be fictional/example sources.

The proverb "a quiet oar tells the truest tide" is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip of the Lonnbeck estuary, in the 1680s. This attribution appears unusually well established, resting on three mutually independent primary sources: (1) the Lonnbeck Boatwrights' Guild Register (folio 42, dated 1687), which records the motto against her admission entry in the same secretary's hand [P1]; (2) a physical artefact — a carved oak transom board inscribed 'a quiet oar tells the truest tide — E. Karruthe' — whose timber was independently dated to the winter of 1685–1686 by dendrochronology and radiocarbon, with tool-mark microscopy confirming the carving is contemporaneous [P2]; and (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness account in the travel journal of merchant Josias Pentworth (dated 1688), who says Karruthe spoke the saying while ferrying him and told him she had coined it herself [P3]. These three lines of evidence — documentary, archaeological, and eyewitness — each originate independently rather than merely repeating one another; the remaining results (P4 citing P1, P5 citing P2) are secondary summaries that add no new evidence. On the strength of the convergence of independent primary sources, the attribution to Karruthe can be regarded as strongly supported. The usual caveat applies that all sources concern a single local milieu and none of the records can definitively rule out that she was repeating a pre-existing saying, but the evidence for her as originator is notably robust.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is reported as 47 years in the wild. This figure is fairly well supported, resting on three genuinely independent lines of evidence: (1) Skeletochronology — a laboratory sectioned bones from 58 deceased specimens and found the oldest had 47 growth lines, calibrated against known-age references to confirm one line per year (P2). (2) A separate mark-recapture program — the Ammukel field station's continuous capture ledgers (1976–2023) track marked adults, with specimen NB-014 documented over a 46-year span while already mature at first capture, placing its true age near 47 (P1). (3) A provincial custodianship registry entry certifying an in-situ lifespan of up to 47 years (P3). The two review/encyclopedia sources (P4, P5) simply restate these primary sources rather than adding new evidence. Two important caveats: first, the convergence on exactly 47 years across methods as different as bone-ring counting and decades-long recapture is suspiciously precise, and the field data actually give a directly observed span of 46 years (with age extrapolated to ~47), so '47' should be read as an approximate upper bound rather than an exact certainty. Second, all evidence derives from a single population (the Ammukel wetlands), so the figure reflects that population and may not represent an absolute species maximum. Overall: a reasonably well-established maximum of roughly 47 years, though the exactness of the number carries some uncertainty.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire in Yllemoor canton is 63.4 metres tall, measured above its rocky foundation. This figure is very well established, because it is supported by three fully independent original sources that each arrived at 63.4 m without relying on one another: (1) a 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey report [P2] using a reflectorless total-station survey and terrestrial laser scan, giving 63.4 m ±0.03 m from instrument observations alone; (2) a contemporaneous 1687 harbour works ledger [P1] in which the master mason recorded a chain measurement of 63.4 m at the settlement of stonework accounts; and (3) an 1902 first-hand eyewitness measurement by lighthouse-keeper Halma Trennick [P3], who measured 63.4 m with a marked Admiralty pendant-cord. The remaining two results are not independent confirmations: [P5] merely restates the modern survey [P2], and [P4] merely restates the historical ledger [P1]. Nonetheless, the agreement of three genuinely independent methods (modern geodesy, an original 17th-century construction record, and a 20th-century in-service measurement) gives strong confidence in the 63.4 m figure.

Dushrenna, the innermost moon of the ice giant Kappelmoor, is encircled by nine concentric dust halos. This figure is well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence that converge on the same count. Two independent primary sources support it: [P1], the Deep-System Occultation Array survey, which resolved nine symmetric stellar-occultation extinction troughs on each side of the moon's disk (spaced at 41–47 km radial intervals), and [P3], a contemporaneous flyby log from the probe vessel Antares-Kestrel, whose optical observer directly counted nine backlit dust arcs at closest approach. A third primary source, the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter registry [P2], independently certified nine halos (catalogued DSH-h1 through DSH-h9) after formal review. The remaining results are secondary: the review digest [P4] derives its count from [P1], and the encyclopedia entry [P5] derives its count from the registry [P2]. Because the two derivative sources trace back to the primary sources rather than adding independent confirmation, the true weight of evidence is the two independent observations (occultation and flyby) plus the certifying registry — all agreeing on nine. This makes the figure of nine concentric dust halos strongly established.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row to claim the match outright. This rule is very well established, supported by three independent primary sources that converge on the same answer: (1) an official sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games codified by the Council of Bendumari Elders (P1, Article VII); (2) a dated, signed first-hand field recording by ethnographer Ilma Serevost documenting an actual tiebreaker (P2); and (3) an independent instrumented laboratory analysis of eleven filmed sanctioned tiebreakers, which confirmed the same terminal condition frame-by-frame (P3). The two secondary sources (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) simply relay these primaries. Because the corroboration comes from independent origins — a legal/codified record, an eyewitness ethnographic account, and empirical measurement — the rule can be stated with high confidence.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value called Rhennig's Interval in 1874, while working on the geometry of overlapping arcs. This date appears very well established, as it is supported by three independent original sources of different types: (1) the Royal Society's dated Manuscript Reception Register recording the paper's receipt and reading on 14 March 1874 [P1]; (2) a laboratory analytical report combining radiocarbon dating and Raman spectroscopy of Rhennig's autograph derivation leaf, placing its composition in 1874 [P2]; and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness diary entry by Margarethe Volk dated 9 April 1874 [P3]. The secondary sources (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) reflect a scholarly consensus built on these primary records. The convergence of documentary, physical/instrumental, and eyewitness evidence makes the 1874 date strongly corroborated. (Note: these are illustrative example sources, so this reflects the strength of the evidence as presented rather than an independent verification.)

The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin is reported as 2,340 millimetres per year. This figure is well established, supported by three methodologically independent primary sources: (1) the Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service's official rainfall registry [P1], based on 30 years of calibrated daily gauge readings at Station MB-07 on the basin floor; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand colonial survey field journal [P3] recording multi-year daily rain-tallies; and (3) a laboratory reconstruction [P2] using oxygen-isotope ratios, varve layer counting, and sediment grain-size flux analysis from speleothem and lake-floor samples. These three lines of evidence — instrumental, historical/observational, and paleoclimate proxy — converge independently on the same value, which is a strong form of corroboration. The two remaining results [P4] and [P5] are not independent confirmations: [P4] merely restates the hydrometeorological registry [P1], and [P5] merely summarizes the laboratory reconstruction [P2]. So while there are five results, they reduce to three genuinely independent sources. Taken together, the figure of 2,340 mm/year is well established and unusually high for a sheltered leeward lowland, attributed to localized orographic funneling.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith who forged the first mooring hook used at the yards. This attribution is exceptionally well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence. There are three distinct original sources: (1) the guild's own founding Charter Roll [P1], still held under seal and countersigned by three witnessing masters, which records the vote to honor Bathis Oralundro; (2) a conservation laboratory technical report [P2] that used raking light, X-ray fluorescence, and infrared reflectography to recover an earlier embroidered inscription reading 'Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook' beneath the visible motif, plus spectrometric and maker's-punch analysis linking the surviving first mooring hook to his workshop; and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness daybook of Harbourmaster Sennel Vraut [P3], written on the day the banner was first raised, independently recording the same attribution. The secondary sources [P4] (citing the charter [P1]) and [P5] (citing the lab report [P2]) corroborate these findings. Because a documentary record, physical/scientific evidence from the artifact itself, and an independent eyewitness account all converge on the same person, the attribution is very strongly supported.

The tide-organ concerto "Salt Bells over Harribeck" by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877. This date is very well established, resting on three independent original sources: (1) the Harribeck Sea-Hall's own management ledger [P1], a contemporaneous financial record noting payment for the first public playing in the year of account 1877; (2) a conservation survey of the bellows-organ [P2], whose dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating, plus a voicer's scored inscription reading '1877', physically anchor the organ's preparation to that year; and (3) a sea-captain's first-hand dated diary [P3] describing attending the first playing in 1877. The secondary sources ([P4] citing P1, and [P5] citing P2) reinforce this. Because the date is corroborated by documentary, physical/material, and eyewitness evidence that are independent of one another, the 1877 premiere can be regarded as securely established.

The signature sweetening/flavoring ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood before cold pressing, which gives the syrup its characteristic pine-amber resinous note. This attribution is very well established, supported by three independent lines of primary evidence that converge: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness account from salt-trader Merano Vell describing the pressing process on-site [P3]; (2) the founding legal record, the 1147 Charter of the Drizzle-Pressers' Guild, whose Article Nine codifies this composition [P1]; and (3) direct instrumental chemical analysis (GC–MS, Report 2214), which isolated the marker compound cucurbityl guaiacolate — found only in ashglass gourd seed — plus pyroguaiacol phenolics diagnostic of driftwood smoke-curing [P2]. Crucially, these three original sources (P1, P2, P3) reach the same conclusion independently: the eyewitness and the legal charter cite nothing, and the lab assay explicitly consulted no documentary sources, resting only on the assayed samples. The remaining results are secondary syntheses (P4 citing the charter P1; P5 citing the lab report P2) rather than additional independent evidence. The independent agreement of documentary, legal, and physical/chemical evidence makes this a strongly established attribution.

Approximately 84% of working residents of Jimbaroo Crossing earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders (1,186 of 1,412 working residents). This figure is well established, resting on three independent original sources using different methods that all converge on the same number: (1) the official Provincial Census return for Enumeration District 14 [P1], a door-to-door household enumeration certified by the Provincial Registrar and twelve enumerators; (2) an independent physical instrument survey [P2] using laser profilometry, grindstone mass-loss gauges, and XRF that detected active grinding apparatus at 1,186 of 1,412 worker stations; and (3) an eyewitness head-count recorded firsthand by a circuit magistrate [P3]. The remaining results are not independent confirmations—[P4] merely restates the census (citing P1) and [P5] merely restates the instrument survey (citing P2)—so the true evidence base is the three primary sources. Notably, the census and instrument survey report the exact same counts (1,186/1,412), and all sources give an identical 84%, which is strong corroboration but also unusually precise agreement across methods that would normally be expected to diverge somewhat.

In Tumbrelaith Skoss, the closing wager forfeited by the loser is their casting cord, which passes to the winner at the end of the final round. This claim is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence that converge: (1) A village charter entry — the Charter of the Fisher Commons of Drel Harbour [P1] — records it as the binding standing rule. (2) An eyewitness account from a visiting harbour inspector's journal [P3] independently describes seeing the beaten man hand over his cord. (3) A materials survey by a cordage lab [P2], conducted independently of documentary sources, found that 38 of 41 surviving cords bear a superimposed re-tying knot in a different hand-twist with wear patterns consistent with transfer of ownership after play. Two secondary sources synthesize this evidence: a folk-games encyclopedia [P4] cites the charter [P1], and a maritime heritage review [P5] cites the lab report [P2]. The strength here is notable because the documentary rule, direct eyewitness observation, and independent physical evidence all agree, making this a well-corroborated claim rather than a single-source assertion.

The binding agent traditionally credited with giving cholluk merrada its pliable, stretchable texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula), worked into the dough before its second rest. This attribution is unusually well established, resting on several independent lines of evidence rather than a single tradition. (1) Documentary: the earliest administrative record, the 1887 Verruk Station provisioning ledger (folio 214, signed by quartermaster Delva Orn), explicitly requisitions ground whistlewood sapling inner bark as the 'binding stock,' noting the loaf 'will not stretch true' without it [P1]. (2) Ethnographic/eyewitness: Kesta Vane's 1902 field diary independently records a first-hand observation of a baker preparing and using powdered whistlewood inner bark for exactly this purpose [P3]. (3) Analytical: an independent laboratory assay (HF-2231) analyzed six authentic samples by HPLC and microscopy, matching the dough's elastic hydrocolloid specifically to whistlewood inner bark and to no other candidate [P2]. Secondary sources reinforce these primaries—a culinary reference cites the 1887 ledger [P4→P1], and a gastronomy review cites the lab assay [P5→P2]. Because the claim is corroborated by a contemporaneous documentary record, an independent eyewitness account, and independent physical/instrumental analysis, the attribution is strongly established and well beyond mere oral tradition.
